CausalChain: Green tea catechins (EGCG) -> Inhibition of redox-sensitive signaling pathways (e.g., NF-κB, EGFR, IGF-I) and modulation of cellular oxidative state -> Inhibition of epigenetic enzymes (DNMTs and HDACs) -> Epigenetic reprogramming of cancer stem cells -> Upregulation of tumor suppressor genes and reduction of chemoresistance -> Enhanced tumor immune infiltration and improved response to cancer therapies
Hypothesis: Chronic consumption of green tea catechins induces epigenetic reprogramming in cancer stem cells via inhibition of DNA methyltransferases and histone deacetylases, thereby reducing their chemoresistance and remodeling the tumor microenvironment to enhance the efficacy of immunotherapeutic and chemotherapeutic interventions.
Abstract: Green tea catechins, particularly epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG), have been largely investigated for their ability to induce apoptosis, inhibit cell proliferation, and modulate key signaling pathways in various cancers. Building upon these well‐documented effects, we propose a novel hypothesis that chronic ingestion of green tea catechins may induce epigenetic reprogramming in cancer stem cells. This reprogramming—mediated by the inhibition of DNA methyltransferases and histone deacetylases—could lead to reactivation of silenced tumor suppressor genes, reduction in chemoresistance, and a remodeled tumor microenvironment favoring immune cell infiltration. In this context, green tea catechins could serve as adjuvants to enhance the effectiveness of conventional chemotherapeutic and immunotherapeutic regimens. Future research aimed at elucidating the epigenetic shifts in cancer stem cell populations upon catechin exposure could provide valuable insights into overcoming therapeutic resistance in aggressive malignancies.
